sm: This is the Friday, November twentieth edition of The World and Everything in It. In the news, President Trump returned from a three-way summit in Shenzhen with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin, where he pressed for nuclear arms reduction. The leaders agreed to keep talking, and also agreed on the need for more global oil supplies. Congress heads into Thanksgiving recess with ten business days to meet a December eleventh funding deadline. Hackers posted contact information for thousands of JP Morgan Chase customers, and a string of tech outages alarmed Americans, though officials say they are unrelated. An Emerson poll shows Marco Rubio at 44 percent among Republicans for 2028, ahead of JD Vance at 24 percent.

On Culture Friday, John Stonestreet of the Colson Center discusses new research on baby names. About a third of American babies had biblical names in 1980, and that is now twenty percent, though obscure biblical names are appearing. A Pew projection says Muslims will outnumber Christians worldwide by 2035. Stonestreet says demographics is destiny, but notes earlier predictions overstated Islam's growth and Christianity has been counted out before. They then turn to a Dallas gathering called Christ Is King America, featuring Alex Jones and Nick Fuentes and organized by Joel Webbon. Stonestreet says its aims include removing Jewish influence from politics, restoring patriarchy, mass deportation and elevating America as a white nation, and he calls it loud and more than noise.

Stonestreet says these ideas are spreading in some churches and college campuses and among young conservative men, reflecting a shift from a politics shaped by Christianity to one shaped by a Nietzschean pursuit of power. He calls it a reverse form of critical theory. Asked about the recent tech outages at Microsoft, the FAA, the NSA, Apple, and banks, he says distrust after COVID makes conspiracy thinking understandable. However, he argues incompetence is a better explanation than conspiracy, since none of the outages lasted long and predicted disruptions never came. He compares it to the Y2K scare, though he admits the timing is suspicious.

Stonestreet says the collapse of trust across Western culture will keep bearing poison fruit. The hosts then discuss a viral Saturday Night Live sketch, with five million views, parodying a free live-in elder care service called Sister. AARP says three in five family caregivers are women. Stonestreet says the sketch reflects real differences between men and women and the difficulty culture has accepting them. He adds that fewer babies will mean fewer siblings to share caregiving, and quotes Stanley Hauerwas that Christians will stand out by caring for the elderly. Next, Colin Garbareno begins a review of the film I Play Rocky, marking fifty years since Rocky, which he calls underrated as a character drama.

Garbareno reviews I Play Rocky, which follows a struggling Sylvester Stallone in 1970s New York. After watching an underdog fight Muhammad Ali, he writes the Rocky script in three and a half days. He refuses to sell it unless he plays the lead, and the producers settle on a budget of just one million dollars. Cost cutting moved the story to Philadelphia, which led to the museum steps scene. Garbareno rates it PG-13, notes some coarse material, calls it his favorite movie of the year, and praises Anthony Ippolito's performance. Then George Grant begins his Quest interview with Chris Larson, head of Ligonier Ministries, who says he is a slow reader and begins with R.C. Sproul's The Holiness of God.

Chris Larson says The Holiness of God, which he studied with his future wife in college, drew him into church history through its chapter on Luther's courage. His second book is G.K. Chesterton's Orthodoxy, especially the chapter on the Ethics of Elfland, which shows standing firm with joy rather than grim endurance. His third is The Lord of the Rings, which shows the cost of battles worth fighting and what Galadriel calls the long defeat. The thread connecting them is that you must stand for what is right and true before you know the outcome. The program then credits its staff and closes with a Bible verse from Psalm 119.
